#10837. Top 5 3D Animation Software in 2026

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Choosing the best 3D animation software depends on your experience, budget, and creative goals. Some tools offer complete 3D modeling and animation workflows, while others specialize in professional character animation, visual effects, or AI-powered video creation. This guide compares five options and notes how each fits into web and game projects, so designers and developers can see which one suits their pipeline.

Blender is one of the strongest free options for anyone looking for comprehensive 3D animation software. This open-source application combines modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, rendering, simulation, and compositing in one package.

Blender provides a broad production workflow without requiring users to pay for a standard commercial license. Its active community, learning resources, and add-on ecosystem make it accessible to independent creators. It is suitable for everything from simple animated scenes to complex short films and game assets.

For web and game developers: Blender ships with a glTF 2.0 importer and exporter, and glTF is the format libraries such as three.js load for 3D on the web. See the Blender manual’s glTF page for export options.

Its extensive interface and feature set can feel overwhelming to new users. Learning advanced rigging, lighting, materials, and rendering takes time, and some established studios may have specialized pipelines built around other applications.

Beginners, freelancers, indie game developers, students, and professionals who need a powerful 3D animation tool without a software subscription.

Autodesk Maya is a professional 3D application widely associated with character animation, rigging, film production, and game development. It offers detailed control over character movement and complex animation workflows, making it a strong choice for artists working in established production environments.

Maya provides sophisticated tools for animating characters and managing complex scenes. Its established role in many professional workflows makes it a valuable skill for artists pursuing careers in film, television, and game development. It also offers detailed control over animation timing, character motion, and rig behavior.

Maya generally requires a paid subscription, which can be expensive for hobbyists and independent creators. Its advanced interface also takes time to learn, particularly for users who have never worked with professional 3D software.

Professional animators, film and television artists, game studios, and users who need advanced character animation and rigging capabilities.

Cinema 4D is a 3D modeling, animation, and rendering application known for its motion graphics workflow. It is widely used for commercial visuals, broadcast graphics, product animations, and creative work that combines 3D elements with graphic design.

Cinema 4D is a strong option for designers who want to create polished motion graphics and branded animation. Its MoGraph workflow can make repetitive or complex movements easier to manage, and its integration with common design workflows is helpful for agencies and creative teams.

For web and product designers: Cinema 4D includes a glTF exporter, which helps when a designer needs to hand a 3D model to a developer for the web. Maxon documents the options on its glTF export settings page.

Cinema 4D is a commercial product, so ongoing licensing costs may be a concern. Although it can handle a wide range of 3D work, users focused on highly specialized character animation or procedural visual effects may prefer tools designed around those workflows.

Motion designers, advertising agencies, broadcast artists, product visualization specialists, and creators who regularly produce animated graphics.

Houdini, developed by SideFX, is a 3D software package known for procedural workflows and advanced visual effects. Rather than relying entirely on manually created steps, artists can build systems that generate and modify complex scenes, simulations, and effects.

Houdini offers exceptional flexibility for technical artists and visual-effects specialists. Procedural workflows make it possible to create reusable systems and adjust complex effects efficiently. Its capabilities are particularly valuable when a project needs detailed simulations or large numbers of interconnected elements.

For game developers: SideFX offers Houdini Engine plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine, which let procedural Houdini assets be used inside those engines. SideFX explains the plugins in its Houdini Engine FAQ.

Houdini has a steep learning curve, especially for beginners who are unfamiliar with node-based workflows. Building effective procedural systems requires patience and technical understanding. While free learning options are available, some commercial uses and advanced workflows require an appropriate paid license.

Visual-effects artists, technical directors, simulation specialists, and experienced 3D creators working on demanding film, television, or game projects.

MagicLight.AI is different from the four tools above. It is an AI-powered video creation platform rather than a traditional 3D application, so it produces finished animated videos, not editable 3D scenes, rigs, or game assets. It is included here for readers who want animated storytelling without building a 3D pipeline. It supports AI-generated characters, scene creation, storyboarding, and voice features.

MagicLight.AI can reduce the time and technical effort needed to create animated videos. It is particularly useful for content creators, educators, marketers, and storytellers who want to focus on the script and final message rather than mastering a complex 3D production pipeline.

MagicLight.AI is not a replacement for dedicated 3D software when you need precise control over mesh topology, character rigs, keyframes, physics, or custom 3D scenes. Creators who need editable 3D assets for games or studio production will need a conventional 3D application such as the ones above.

Content creators, educators, and marketers who want to produce animated videos efficiently without learning a traditional 3D animation workflow.

The right software is the one that supports your actual production needs. Before choosing a tool, consider the following factors.

If you want to model objects, build character rigs, and control animation precisely, start with a dedicated 3D application such as Blender or Maya. If your goal is to create animated storytelling videos from scripts or ideas with less manual production work, an AI video tool such as MagicLight.AI may be a more convenient option.

Blender is an excellent starting point if you need a complete 3D toolset without a standard license fee. Houdini also has a free Apprentice edition with restrictions. Maya and Cinema 4D are commercial applications, so compare their current plans against your expected usage before committing.

Different applications suit different workflows. Blender is versatile, Maya excels at character animation, Cinema 4D is well suited to motion graphics, and Houdini is especially powerful for procedural effects. MagicLight.AI is better suited to AI-assisted video production than to detailed, manually controlled 3D scene creation.

Beginners may find Blender’s extensive learning resources helpful, although its broad feature set takes time to master. Maya and Houdini demand more specialized skills for advanced work, while Cinema 4D is often considered by motion designers seeking a more direct design-oriented workflow. AI video tools can reduce the amount of technical setup required, but still require creative direction and review.

Think about where the finished animation will be used. A web project may need a lightweight glTF model. A game project may require exportable 3D assets, rig compatibility, and a game-engine workflow. A commercial motion graphic may depend on rendering and compositing integration. A social video or animated explainer may prioritize turnaround time, narration, subtitles, and scene continuity.

The best 3D animation software in 2026 depends on your budget, experience, and intended output. Blender is the strongest starting point for many users who want a comprehensive free 3D workflow. Autodesk Maya is a compelling option for professional character animation, Cinema 4D suits motion graphics and commercial visuals, and Houdini stands out for procedural effects and complex simulations. MagicLight.AI offers a different approach: it helps creators generate animated videos with AI rather than manually building a traditional 3D production pipeline.

Blender is one of the best free options because it includes modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and other production tools in a single open-source application. It is suitable for beginners as well as experienced artists.

Yes. Free software can support professional-quality work when used effectively. Blender, for example, provides a comprehensive toolset for animation and rendering. The final result depends on the artist’s skills, project requirements, hardware, and production workflow.

Blender is a strong choice for beginners who want to learn traditional 3D modeling and animation without paying for a standard software license. Those who mainly want to create animated videos from stories or scripts may prefer exploring an AI video creation platform such as MagicLight.AI.

Blender and Cinema 4D can both export glTF, a format widely used for 3D on the web. Blender is free, so it is the easiest place to start.

#10836. Call of Duty player says $280 Asus monitor saved them from stray bullet fired outside house

A Call of Duty player claims their Asus gaming monitor saved their life after a stray bullet flew through their wall and struck their screen during a late-night gaming session.

Reddit user ‘antisocialnae’ shared their terrifying experience on November 2, revealing how a $280 Asus TUF gaming monitor they purchased five years ago may have prevented a tragedy.

According to the player, they were enjoying some late-night Call of Duty when they suddenly heard loud bangs coming from outside. Unlike the gunfire in their game, these shots were very real.

Realizing something was wrong, they immediately dropped to the floor and called 911.

After speaking with the operator, the player checked their wall and discovered a bullet hole directly behind their gaming setup. Even more frightening, the bullet had struck their main monitor, but there was no exit hole.

“I couldn’t believe the monitor held the round in from possibly hitting me head on, hurting me really badly, or absolutely destroying my PC build depending on the trajectory it was going,” they explained.

The monitor in question was an Asus TUF VG258QM 280Hz display, which they purchased for $280 when building their first gaming setup five years earlier.

Understandably, the ordeal left them shaken.

“I cried so much when everything calmed down and I realized how close I was to meeting my maker,” they admitted.

Fortunately, they still have two other Asus monitors, although they hadn’t turned their PC back on to check whether it survived the incident.

PC saves woman’s life by deflecting a bullet while she sleeps

Twitch streamer’s gaming monitor stops bullet and keeps working

Apex Legends player nearly dies IRL after stray bullet hits his monitor

The story is remarkably similar to a 2022 incident involving an Apex Legends YouTuber, whose monitor was struck by a bullet that reportedly missed his head by just three inches.

The incident quickly caught the attention of Asus, with a company representative responding directly to the Reddit thread.

“While we pride ourselves on making durable monitors and making gaming seem lifelike, your monitor definitely went above and beyond in both regards,” they wrote.

“We’ll reach out to you soon to see what we can do to honor its sacrifice.”

Naturally, someone had to ask the important question: “I take it as the warranty doesn’t cover stray 9mm rounds?”

The Asus representative joked that the damage would normally fall under customer-induced damage or an “act of god,” but suggested the unusual circumstances might warrant special consideration.

“Doesn’t mean we can support, but if you do customer service long enough, there are cases that obviously stand out from the rest,” they explained.

A replacement has not been confirmed, but the player already has a pretty good excuse for an upgrade.

And bizarrely, this isn’t the first time gaming hardware has taken a bullet for its owner in 2026. Back in June, a woman credited her gaming PC with saving her life after it deflected a shot fired through her neighbor’s wall.

#10834. GTA 6 fan who went viral for hoping to live long enough to play the game has died

A 25-year-old GTA 6 fan who captured the attention of the gaming community after sharing his wish to live long enough to play Rockstar Games’ upcoming title has died.

The fan had been battling interstitial lung disease since he was 17 years old, with his condition eventually deteriorating to the point that he needed a lung transplant.

His family confirmed that he died on October 29, 2026, following a series of infections and worsening health complications, just months after supporters rallied around his story and raised thousands of dollars to help with his medical treatment.

In a TikTok update shared on November 2, a family member revealed that he had developed a severe infection several weeks before his death, causing his lungs to fill with blood.

Doctors reportedly informed the family that he was unlikely to survive and presented hospice care as an option. However, he initially chose to continue treatment, remaining on life support equipment that included ECMO, a machine used to support heart and lung function.

His condition continued to deteriorate, and on October 28, he told his family that he was ready to stop fighting.

The following morning, his loved ones received a call informing them that another infection had developed overnight. His blood work had worsened, and his organs were beginning to shut down.

Family members returned to his bedside, where they found that he was no longer responsive as he had been the previous day.

“He was peaceful. He was at peace. He was peaceful. He was so peaceful,” the family member said. “And he’s no longer fighting. He’s no longer hurting. He’s no longer struggling.”

Daughter makes emotional plea to Rockstar so terminally ill dad can play GTA 6

GTA 6 fans raise $50k for sick fan trying to live long enough to play VI

GTA 6 fan emails Rockstar asking for poster and actually gets one

His mother, Paris Fort, had previously organized a GoFundMe campaign titled “Help My Son Reach His Lung Transplant,” seeking financial assistance for his treatment and recovery.

The fundraiser explained that he had been living with interstitial lung disease for eight years and needed a transplant after his condition worsened.

Donations were intended to help cover transplant-related expenses, relocation, and recovery costs. The campaign ultimately raised more than $96,000 from approximately 5,000 donations, far exceeding its original $15,000 goal.

In the announcement of his death, the family thanked supporters for helping make his final months memorable.

“He was so happy. He felt like his dreams were coming true, and he wanted to give back like y’all gave to him,” the family member explained.

Beyond his wish to play GTA 6, he had also hoped to share his music with a wider audience.

“All he wanted was to push his music out and to be known and for people to hear his voice,” the family member said.

His family is now planning a balloon release for supporters, although a date has not yet been announced.

The video concluded with another message of appreciation for everyone who supported him throughout his medical battle.

“Thank y’all for making his last few months beautiful.”

#10831. Tech multimillionaire and family identified among victims of Florida private jet crash

Tech multimillionaire Adam Robinson, his wife, and their two young children have been identified among the nine people who died in a devastating private jet crash in Florida.

The Learjet 60 was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday, November 1, when it suddenly plummeted from the sky and crashed into a residential area in Palm Beach County at approximately 12:50 p.m.

The aircraft exploded on impact, leaving a massive crater in the ground and scattering debris across the surrounding neighborhood. All nine people on board died.

According to TMZ, 44-year-old tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson was traveling with his wife, Helen Sharp, their two children, a nanny, and two close friends.

Robinson was the founder of Retention.com and RB2B, two marketing technology companies specializing in customer identification and sales leads. Before entering the tech industry, he worked in finance at Lehman Brothers and Barclays Capital.

WATCH: New video shows Learjet 60 business jet crashing near West Palm Beach, Florida.The plane was completely disintegrated upon impact. Number of casualties unknown. pic.twitter.com/l5JT9KEWnQ

The entrepreneur previously built email marketing company Robly, which he reportedly sold in an eight-figure deal.

As People reported, the couple’s children were identified as four-year-old Emma and two-year-old Charlie.

Their nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina, and family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were also among those killed.

In a statement, relatives described Emma and Charlie as “the light of their lives.”

The aircraft’s two pilots were identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory and 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, who reportedly earned her pilot’s license at just 17 years old.

Millionaire tech CEO dies after private jet crashes into car on Texas highway

Pilot responds after miraculously landing in Atlantic Ocean without hurting anyone

Pan Am plane lost for 74 years finally found on Atlantic Ocean floor

Moments before the crash, air traffic control recordings captured the crew reporting ice accumulation and moderate turbulence while requesting permission to climb to a higher altitude.

However, the situation rapidly deteriorated, with the aircraft descending at more than 20,000 feet per minute as the pilots desperately attempted to regain control.

The crew’s final radio transmissions included a warning that they were going to crash before the words, “We’re out of time.”

The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation into the crash. Officials say there is evidence the aircraft may have begun breaking apart before impact, although the exact cause remains unknown.

The tragedy comes just months after another prominent Austin entrepreneur, Capital Factory CEO Joshua Baer, died in a separate private jet crash in June 2026.

#10830. How to Test Location-Aware APIs with FastAPI and PostGIS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Catch coordinate-order bugs, distance mistakes, boundary cases, and bad spatial assumptions before they reach production.

A location endpoint can return HTTP 200 and still be wrong by kilometers. That is the uncomfortable part of testing geospatial APIs: ordinary API checks tell you whether the request worked, not whether the geography is correct.

Spatial bugs can look harmless in code review. Latitude and longitude get reversed. A radius value is treated as degrees instead of meters. A query works near one city but behaves differently elsewhere because the geometry column uses the wrong type. The JSON is valid, the tests are green, and the map is still wrong.

In this tutorial, you will build a small FastAPI endpoint backed by PostGIS and then test the spatial behavior directly. The examples use deterministic fixtures positioned at known distances, so the tests verify geography rather than only response structure.

The API exposes one endpoint: GET /places/nearby. A client sends longitude, latitude, and a radius in meters. The service returns nearby places as GeoJSON features, ordered by distance.

The useful part is not the endpoint itself. The useful part is the test strategy. We will check coordinate validation, exact distance boundaries, GeoJSON coordinate order, and the database query that turns a radius into a spatial filter.

Use a geography column when the API is answering human-scale distance questions in meters. PostGIS can then calculate on the ellipsoid instead of treating longitude and latitude as flat Cartesian coordinates.

The endpoint below validates longitude, latitude, and radius with Pydantic, then sends a parameterized query to PostgreSQL. The SQL uses ST_DWithin to filter candidates and ST_Distance to return the measured distance.

The API accepts lon and lat as separate named parameters. That removes ambiguity at the HTTP boundary. GeoJSON still uses [longitude, latitude] when the response is created.

Hard-coding two real businesses and hoping their distance is approximately right makes a fragile test. A better approach is to create test points at exact distances from a fixed origin.

PostGIS can generate those fixtures with ST_Project. In the test database, create one point 500 meters away, one 950 meters away, and one 1,500 meters away. Now a 1,000-meter query has an unambiguous expected result: the first two belong in the response and the third does not.

This is the first test that actually proves something spatial. It is not checking that the endpoint returns a list. It is checking that the 1-kilometer contract means what the API says it means.

GeoJSON coordinates are longitude first, latitude second. Many developers naturally think latitude first because that is how coordinates are commonly spoken. A validation layer can catch the most obvious reversal before the database ever sees it.

Longitude must be between -180 and 180. Latitude must be between -90 and 90. That will not catch every reversal, because both numbers may sometimes fall inside both ranges, but it catches a large class of failures and gives clients a useful error instead of a misleading map.

A response can be syntactically valid JSON and still violate the GeoJSON contract. Assert the geometry type and the coordinate order. For a known query point, longitude should appear in element zero and latitude in element one.

Spatial boundaries deserve their own tests. A place at 999 meters should be included in a 1,000-meter search. A place at 1,001 meters should not. A place exactly at the boundary should behave consistently with the predicate you chose.

ST_DWithin includes features whose distance is less than or equal to the supplied threshold, so document that behavior and test it explicitly.

Unit tests are useful for request validation, but mocking the repository layer removes the most important part of this API: PostGIS itself. Keep a small integration-test database and run at least a few tests against the real extension.

That catches mistakes that mocks cannot: geography versus geometry behavior, SRID mismatches, spatial indexes, units, and changes to SQL functions. A location API is one of the cases where a cheap database integration test buys a lot of confidence.

Correctness is only half the story. A radius endpoint that scans every feature will work in development and become painful at production scale. Add a GiST index and inspect the query plan.

The exact plan depends on your data and PostgreSQL version, but you should see the spatial index participating in candidate filtering. Treat an accidental sequential scan on a large production table as a regression worth investigating.

For a real project, I would split the tests into two groups. Fast validation tests run on every commit. PostGIS integration tests run in CI with a temporary PostgreSQL/PostGIS service.

The CI gate should cover invalid coordinates, zero or negative radius values, known-distance fixtures, boundary behavior, GeoJSON output, and at least one query-plan or performance sanity check for larger datasets.

This is more work than asserting status_code == 200, but it tests the thing users actually care about: whether the API's answer is geographically true.

Location APIs fail in ways ordinary web tests are not designed to notice. The response can have the right schema, the database call can succeed, and every field can look reasonable while the location itself is wrong.

The fix is not a giant testing framework. Start with a few spatial invariants you can prove: known distances, valid coordinate ranges, correct GeoJSON order, deterministic boundary behavior, and real PostGIS integration tests. Those checks turn geography from an assumption into something your CI pipeline can verify.

#10828. Dead by Daylight removes TheBurntPeanut’s free DLC following backlash

Dead by Daylight developer Behaviour Interactive has removed the free content gifted to Twitch streamer TheBurntPeanut, admitting its handling of the controversy has “broken trust” with the community.

On October 30, Twitch streamer TheBurntPeanut was granted access to all Dead by Daylight’s DLC characters and perks during a livestream. The move sparked controversy in the community, with many fans raising concerns about the decision.

After an initial response on November 1, the devs have published a longer statement through the official Dead by Daylight X account, confirming the content had been removed and outlining changes to how it works with creators.

According to the November 3 statement, members of the team noticed a large audience watching a streamer who had not played Dead by Daylight before and saw an opportunity to welcome new players.

However, the decision to grant content and participate in the streamer’s chat happened without the usual team discussions or checks.

“When collaborating with a new creator, we normally look thoroughly at their past content to determine whether they are representing the values of inclusion our community expects from us,” Behaviour explained. “In this case, this was not taken into proper consideration or discussed as a group.”

Behaviour also addressed its official account’s response after the streamer offered to return the content, saying its “WE CAN TAKE THE HEAT!” message had escalated the situation.

“This message, along with some others in that session, showed a disregard for the context we were suddenly in and crossed the line of appropriate responses from our brand,” the statement continued. “That reply escalated the situation for us and for our community, especially our content creators on the frontlines of these conversations, and that’s unacceptable.”

Dead by Daylight team respond following backlash to TheBurntPeanut receiving free DLC

Dead by Daylight players slam devs over NFT Hellraiser collection

Dead by Daylight rolls back healing system changes after community backlash

To our community:We wanted to follow up on yesterday’s message to better address the questions you are actually asking and that matter most to you. pic.twitter.com/OPqAJ9xIoh

The developer confirmed it had already removed the gifted content and was rewriting its guidelines for interacting with creators, including deciding who on the team can authorize these decisions.

These updated guidelines will focus on identifying creators whose past conduct conflicts with the inclusive community Behaviour says it wants to build. Approval procedures for granting content and currency will also be updated, alongside staff training and communication standards.

Addressing questions about the employees involved, Behaviour said it was “taking appropriate action internally,” but would not share further details because the matter is confidential.

“This incident has broken trust with our community, who hold expectations and regard for the types of people we partner with, but more importantly, expectations of the conduct and actions taken by our team in our daily work within this community,” explained the devs.

“We understand it will be a slow road to regain that trust, but we are committed to doing the work necessary to get there.”

#10821. 7 Checks Developers Should Make So AI Search Can Read Their Site

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Search results now include AI-written answers that cite pages, and people increasingly ask chat tools for recommendations instead of scrolling a list of links. For developers, this does not mean learning a new discipline. It means making sure the basics are in place so that crawlers and answer engines can reach, read and quote your pages.

Most problems are plain engineering mistakes: a blocked crawler, a page that renders nothing without JavaScript, or markup that disagrees with the visible text. This article covers seven checks, including one script you can run against your own robots.txt.

AI features in search do not need a special file or a special format. Google's documentation on AI features and your website states that a page needs to be indexed and eligible to appear in Search with a snippet, and that there are no additional technical requirements. It also says there is no need for new AI-specific files or special schema.org markup.

So start with the fundamentals. Check for accidental noindex tags after a deploy, confirm important pages return a 200 status, and make sure staging settings never reach production.

Answer engines read text. If your key information lives in images, canvas elements or content that only appears after a client-side script runs, a crawler may never see it. View the page source and the rendered HTML, and compare them. Product names, prices, definitions and steps should be present as real text.

Structured data helps systems understand a page, but only if it agrees with what visitors see. SitePoint's guide to JSON-LD for developers shows how to build markup that search and AI systems can parse. Generate it from the same data that renders the page, and validate it after every template change. Markup that contradicts the visible text is worse than no markup.

Your robots.txt decides which crawlers may fetch your pages. Some sites block AI crawlers deliberately, and others block them by accident through a broad rule. SitePoint's technical guide to working with a marketing agency lists robots.txt decisions about which crawlers may access the site among the checks developers should own.

This small function reads a robots.txt string and reports which common AI-related crawlers are blocked from the whole site:

Run it against your live robots.txt. If a crawler appears in the list and you did not intend that, fix the rule. Note that blocking a crawler is a legitimate choice. The goal is that it is a decision and not an accident.

Developers can check access and markup, but judging how a brand shows up in AI answers often needs someone who tracks that area full time. An AI search consultant such as Austin Heaton works on answer engine optimization.

Traffic from AI features in Google Search is included in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Set up that report, tag your own campaigns with consistent UTM parameters, and watch referral traffic from chat tools in your analytics. You cannot control the answers, but you can see whether clicks arrive.

Most visibility problems appear after a deployment: a template change drops the structured data, a new rule blocks a crawler, or a redesign hides text behind a script. Add a small post-deploy test for the checks above. A failing robots.txt check or a missing JSON-LD block should stop the release before a crawler finds the problem.

Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup for AI search? Google's documentation says no new AI-specific files or special structured data are needed for its AI features. Standard indexing and crawling requirements apply.

Should I block AI crawlers? That depends on your goals. Blocking is a legitimate choice, but make it deliberately and review it regularly.

Where do I see AI search traffic? For Google, AI feature traffic is counted in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Other tools show up as referrals in your analytics.

Making a site readable to AI search is mostly ordinary engineering: keep pages indexable, put key content in text, keep structured data consistent, decide crawler access on purpose, measure what you can and retest after every release. The robots.txt check above is small, but it catches one of the most common accidental blocks before it costs you visibility.

#10819. Spanish footballer dies aged 30 after collision with goalkeeper during match

Spanish footballer Jesús de Miguel has died aged 30 after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision with an opposing goalkeeper during a match.

The Tenerife forward was struck in the chest while challenging for the ball against Andorra on Monday, November 2, during a Spanish second division match at Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López.

De Miguel collapsed on the pitch, prompting players from both teams to urgently call for medical assistance.

Medical staff treated the 30-year-old for more than five minutes before he was rushed to hospital by ambulance. The match was subsequently abandoned.

Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, who was involved in the collision, was shown a straight red card.

Tenerife confirmed that De Miguel’s neurological condition had deteriorated in the hours following the incident, before announcing his death on Tuesday morning.

“Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00 am, of Jesús de Miguel Alameda.” the club said in a statement, translated from Spanish.

“There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness. We stand alongside his devastated family, alongside his loved ones, alongside all of tinerfeñismo that today weeps for this cruel outcome.”

De Miguel began his professional career with Leganés B in 2015 and went on to represent eight other Spanish clubs before joining Tenerife in 2025.

His death has prompted tributes from across Spanish football, including messages from Barcelona, Real Madrid, and Andorra.

Barcelona said: “Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times.”

Real Madrid expressed its “condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones.”

#10814. Pokemon collector reveals $660,000 “dream card” was actually fake

A Pokemon collector has revealed that they spent over $600,000 on their “dream card,” only to find out that it was actually a fake slab.

Collecting Pokemon cards has remained a big business over the last few years, with people regularly spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to get their hands on cards from their childhood.

In the case of Jesse Peng, he has been chasing a Call of Legends Shiny Rayquaza card from 2011. He managed to pick up a PSA 10 version for over $660,000, and everything seemed to be above board. However, after doing some investigative work into the card’s background, the Pokemon collector discovered that it was, in fact, a fake.

“It looked like a very clean card and the label looked very very real,” he said, noting the transaction happened through a “well respect middle man” in the TCG world.

“This is so clean that it’s a little bit suspicious to me,” he added, noting that his own system flagged it as fake. “The card is real, the label is real, the only thing that they couldn’t do is get the fugitive ink right.”

Peng said that the “fugitive ink” on the slab doesn’t match the authentic version on other cards in his collection.

“Greed has destroyed our hobby over the last few months and this is not the hobby that I fell in love with 25 years ago,” Peng added, noting that there is a part of him that wants to quit collecting.

The owner of PDGR noted that he has the resources to fight the problem and is “coming after you scammers,” with his app and verification technology.

#10810. Stop Overpaying for App Builders: How to Build Premium Websites and Web Apps with AI

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a professional website or web application no longer requires a large development budget. AI coding agents have changed how developers approach design, development, and deployment. Yet many founders and freelancers still assume they need to pay for a dedicated AI app builder before they can create something polished.

Visual app builders such as Lovable and Bolt can help users turn ideas into working prototypes quickly. Their convenience is valuable, especially for beginners. However, subscriptions, usage limits, and additional services can increase the cost of building and maintaining a project.

There is another approach: use AI coding agents with a development stack you control.

I discovered this firsthand when I moved beyond WordPress development and built a CRM from scratch.

Instead of relying on a dedicated app builder, I used Claude, Next.js, Firebase Firestore, Tailwind CSS, Git, and Vercel.

The experience changed how I think about the cost of building software.

App builders reduce the technical barriers to software development. You describe what you want, and the platform generates interfaces, application logic, and sometimes database integrations.

The problem is not the tools themselves. It is assuming that a paid app builder is the only practical way to build a professional product.

Consider what happens when a project grows. You may need more iterations, additional integrations, more control over the generated code, or a different deployment setup. Depending on the platform and plan, these requirements can introduce additional costs or constraints.

There is also a difference between creating a prototype and building a maintainable application. Generating a dashboard is relatively straightforward. Ensuring that its permissions, database operations, error handling, and security work correctly requires additional engineering.

Paying for an app builder does not automatically solve these problems.

Before subscribing to another platform, ask a more useful question: Am I paying for a capability I genuinely need, or am I paying for a workflow I could manage directly?

I have designed more than 100 websites and helped clients implement over 12 CRM and ERP systems. My experience gave me a strong understanding of website design, business workflows, and the practical problems software needs to solve.

However, configuring existing platforms is different from developing an application from scratch.

When I decided to build a CRM, I wanted to learn the entire process, from writing code to managing data and deploying the application. I also wanted to avoid spending money on a dedicated app-builder subscription when I could use AI coding tools with a more flexible development environment.

I chose Claude as my AI coding agent and used a stack built around Next.js, Firebase Firestore, Tailwind CSS, Git, and Vercel.

This approach helped me move from requirements to implementation without depending on a single visual app-building platform. I also saved more than $1,000 in potential app-builder costs and related expenses compared with the approach I had considered.

That figure reflects my own project and spending decisions. It is not a guarantee that every developer will save the same amount.

More importantly, I gained practical experience with API integrations, application security, performance, and user experience. Those lessons became part of my technical portfolio.

You do not need to reproduce my exact stack for every project. The important idea is to choose tools that work together and give you an appropriate level of control.

An AI coding agent can help generate components, implement features, explain unfamiliar code, and investigate errors.

I used Claude to accelerate implementation and work through development challenges. Instead of asking it to build the entire application in one prompt, I worked through smaller tasks, reviewed the output, and refined the results.

The developer still needs to understand the requirements and verify the generated code. AI can accelerate development, but it cannot guarantee correctness.

Next.js provided the framework for building the web application. It supports structured development, routing, and different approaches to rendering and application logic.

For developers who want more control than a visual builder provides, working directly with a framework also makes it easier to understand how the application is organized.

Firestore provided the database layer for my project. Its document-based data model and integration with the Firebase ecosystem made it a practical choice for the application.

However, using a managed database does not eliminate the need to design data structures carefully, configure access rules, and evaluate query performance as usage grows.

A premium-looking interface depends on more than colors and typography. Spacing, consistency, responsiveness, accessibility, and clear user flows all influence the result.

Tailwind CSS helped me build and refine the interface using utility classes, making iterative design changes easier to manage.

Git allowed me to track changes, review revisions, and recover from problematic updates. Vercel provided the deployment environment and a convenient workflow for connecting releases to the codebase.

Together, these tools supported a development process that was not tied to a dedicated app-builder subscription.

A low-cost stack is only useful if the development process is disciplined.

Start by defining the application's purpose, primary users, and essential features. Then create a simple design system covering typography, spacing, colors, buttons, forms, and navigation.

Build one feature at a time. Ask the AI agent to explain its implementation, review important changes, and test each feature before expanding the application.

For a website, pay attention to responsive layouts, accessibility, loading speed, and search engine requirements. For a web application, also test authentication, permissions, database operations, and error handling.

Finally, deploy early enough to test the application in a realistic environment. Keep the code in version control and make sure you understand how to update, maintain, and recover the application.

These steps matter more than choosing whichever AI tool is currently receiving the most attention.

No. App builders can be excellent choices when speed, simplicity, and minimal setup matter most.

A founder validating an idea may benefit from launching a prototype quickly. A nontechnical user may prefer a managed platform over maintaining a codebase. A team may also find that a paid subscription costs less than the time required to manage its own development environment.

The right decision depends on the project.

If you need extensive customization, want direct control over your code, or expect to develop the application further, an AI coding agent combined with a conventional development stack may offer greater flexibility.

Compare the total cost of ownership rather than the subscription price alone. Include development time, hosting, database usage, API costs, security, maintenance, and the effort required to change platforms later.

AI has made software development more accessible, but accessibility does not mean every project needs another subscription.

My experience building a CRM taught me that a coding agent, a well-chosen technology stack, and a structured development process can be a practical alternative to a dedicated app builder.

The goal should not be to avoid spending money at all costs. It should be to spend where the investment creates genuine value.

Before paying for another tool, explore what you can accomplish with AI-assisted coding and tools you control. You may discover that the biggest limitation is not your budget, but your willingness to learn a different way of building.

Build with the tools that fit your project—not simply the tools that make the first demo easiest.

#10808. Thieves steal 5,000 endangered ants from nature reserve in bizarre theft

Thieves have stolen an entire colony of rare ants from a protected nature reserve, with as many as 5,000 insects potentially taken.

The colony of narrow-headed ants was removed from the reserve in Devon, England, the species’ “last stronghold” in the country.

The theft was discovered during routine checks in mid-October, when researchers found a hole where one of the nests had previously been.

According to Devon Wildlife Trust, the ground around the missing nest showed signs of digging with a spade, suggesting someone had deliberately removed the colony.

A single narrow-headed ant nest can contain between 1,000 and 5,000 ants, including breeding queens that can live for up to 25 years. However, the exact number taken remains unknown.

The species was once much more widespread across England, but habitat loss has reduced its population to a single remaining location. Small numbers also survive in Scotland.

Julia Balfour, a species recovery officer at Devon Wildlife Trust, explained that the loss of even one colony could have lasting consequences.

“The removal of an established nest is a significant loss for this species. Narrow-headed Ant colonies develop slowly, and each mature nest, with its long-lived queens, represents many years of growth that cannot quickly be replaced,” she said.

“Our most recent survey recorded 142 active nests on the nature reserve, so every nest matters. This is the last population of Narrow-headed Ants in England, and losing even one colony sets back years of careful work by our staff, volunteers and partners.”

The theft has been reported to police, who warned that damaging or disturbing a protected nature reserve is a criminal offense.

“Sites of Special Scientific Interest are legally protected, and it is a criminal offence for any person to intentionally or recklessly damage, destroy, or disturb the protected area.”

“If you’ve seen anything suspicious in recent weeks or have any information that may assist us with our investigation, please contact us.”

Steam has become increasingly crowded in recent years, with thousands of games arriving on Valve’s PC storefront every month. As the use of generative AI becomes more widespread, some developers are concerned about how it’s affecting smaller studios.

Now, publisher 2 Left Thumbs has accused Steam’s approval process of damaging the release of its new co-op game, Wheel Make It.

Developed by tlproductions, Wheel Make It is a physics-based game where two players control the wheels of a single wheelchair, working together to navigate obstacles. It was originally scheduled to launch on October 12, but problems during Steam’s review process prevented it from releasing on time.

Further complications followed, with the game eventually launching on November 1. However, despite accumulating more than 11,000 wishlists, it peaked at just 15 concurrent players in the 24 hours after release.

#10792. 7 Engineering Patterns for Measuring Traffic From AI Search and Chat Tools

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

More visitors now arrive from chat assistants and AI answer boxes, but many analytics setups still lump them into "direct" or "referral". Teams then argue about whether AI search matters, using numbers that cannot answer the question.

Measuring this traffic is an engineering task. You need to capture the referrer, classify it, store it safely and know where the data is blind. This article covers seven patterns, including a small classifier you can run.

Explicit tags are more reliable than guessing from a referrer. If you control a link, such as a partner mention or a newsletter, add a standard utm_source and record it on landing. SitePoint's tutorial on building a campaign attribution tracking system covers capturing UTM parameters, storing first-touch and last-touch data, and keeping conversions with no attribution marked as unattributed. Tagged visits should always win over inferred ones.

Browsers limit what they send. MDN's reference for the Referrer-Policy header explains that the default, strict-origin-when-cross-origin, sends only the origin for cross-origin requests over HTTPS and sends no referrer when moving from HTTPS to HTTP.

Keep the classification logic in one place, with a list of known sources that you can update. This function checks for a campaign tag first, then falls back to the referrer hostname, and labels missing referrers as direct or unknown:

The domain list will change as tools appear and rename themselves, so review it regularly. The exact-match check also prevents a lookalike domain such as notchatgpt.com from being counted.

Save the raw classification inputs, the referrer origin and the campaign tag, next to the result. When the domain list changes, you can reclassify old data. Keep raw events for a limited time and aggregated numbers longer. Avoid storing full IP addresses or fingerprints, since you do not need them for this question.

Analytics can show that visits arrive, but explaining why a brand appears in an AI answer, or what to change in content, is a separate specialty. Compare any outside recommendation with the traffic you can measure yourself.

A good report states what it cannot see. Many AI answers are read without a click, some visits carry no referrer, and Search Console reports AI feature clicks together with other web results. Put those limits at the top of the dashboard. A number with its caveats is more useful than a confident chart that hides them.

Can I identify every visit that comes from an AI tool?

No. Some tools send a referrer and some do not, so your numbers will undercount. Use campaign tags wherever you control the link.

Should I use UTM parameters for AI traffic?

Only where you control the link. You cannot tag a link that a chat tool generates on its own.

Keep it only as long as you need to reclassify and audit, for example about 30 days, and keep aggregated metrics longer.

Measuring AI search traffic comes down to honest data handling: define your questions, prefer explicit campaign tags, understand the limits of the referrer, classify visits in one tested function, store auditable events, bring in specialist advice where you need it, and report the blind spots. The classifier above is short, but it makes the logic explicit so you can review and improve it as new tools appear.

I ran into this problem while working with browser-based Unicode text tools. At first, it looks like a typography issue. It is really a text-processing issue.

What users call a “fancy font” is often not a font at all. The text may contain Unicode characters from blocks such as Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols.

That distinction matters anywhere your application searches, validates, sorts, stores, compares, truncates, or assigns meaning to user-entered text.

The solution is not simply “normalize everything”.

You need to decide which representation to preserve, which representation to search, and which representation is safe to use as an identifier.

They look closely related to a person, but JavaScript sees different code points.

The styled letters are not ordinary Latin h, e, l, l, and o with a CSS font applied to them.

This distinction is the heart of a reliable Unicode strategy:

Preserve the original representation for display, but derive another representation for matching when necessary.

For applications with persistent data, I prefer a dual-representation approach.

You preserve the user's original formatting while making search behavior much more predictable.

It also moves normalization work to the write path rather than repeating the same transformation across every record during every search.

For a small browser-only application, normalizing at query time may be perfectly fine.

For a database-backed application with a growing dataset, generating searchable text when content is created or updated is often easier to scale.

The point is to stop pretending every part of your application needs the same representation of the text.

Characters such as mathematical bold letters are part of the string itself. Removing a CSS font does not turn them back into ASCII.

Normalization and text segmentation solve different problems.

Many Unicode bugs stay invisible until a user enters accented text, emoji, combining marks, mathematical symbols, or another writing system.

Styled Unicode text uses separate Unicode characters that visually resemble bold, italic, script, monospace, or other letter styles.

Unlike CSS typography, the appearance is encoded partly in the characters themselves.

Because visually similar strings may contain different Unicode code points.

No, NFKC can intentionally change compatibility characters.

It is often useful for search, matching, or certain identifiers, but it may be destructive for text that should preserve the user's original appearance.

For display content, preserve the original.

If your application needs normalized search or matching, consider storing or generating a separate searchable representation.

They are better when your requirement is genuinely Unicode-aware.

For example, \p{Letter} can match letters from many writing systems.

That does not mean every matched character should automatically be allowed in security-sensitive identifiers.

Normalization can collapse some equivalent or compatibility forms, but visually confusable characters across scripts require separate identifier and security policies.

The biggest Unicode mistake is not using the wrong JavaScript method.

It is giving every string in your application the same rules.

A search index is not the original content.

A character counter is not a storage limit.

Once you separate those responsibilities, styled Unicode becomes much easier to handle.

Normalize what the system needs to match.

Restrict what must function as a secure identifier.

Segment what the interface needs to count.

And before shipping, paste something stranger than “Hello world” into the form.

That small habit catches an surprising number of text bugs before your users do.

#10781. Indie game platform itch.io says it deleted “a couple terabytes” of AI slop

Indie game platform itch.io has revealed that it deleted several terabytes of AI-generated content from its website as concerns grow over the increasing number of games being created using artificial intelligence.

The platform, which allows independent developers to upload and distribute their games, has guidelines restricting excessive amounts of automatically generated content, including projects created with minimal human involvement.

The announcement comes as other gaming storefronts face similar concerns. A recent analysis found that nearly half of all new games released on Steam in October 2026 disclosed using AI-generated content.

“Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop,” itch.io wrote in a November 2 post on X, which attracted more than 1.6 million views.

The platform did not specify how many games or projects were affected or provide details about the individual uploads that were deleted.

Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌

Under its existing quality guidelines, itch.io warns developers against using automated systems to mass-produce product pages, which it considers spam.

This includes games predominantly created by AI with minimal human involvement, randomly generated content with little curated design, and multiple versions of essentially identical AI-generated projects.

Developers are also required to disclose their use of generative AI through a dedicated section on their project’s editing page. Those that do so are listed under an “AI Assisted” browsing category.

However, the platform does not prohibit all uses of AI. Its guidelines state that developers can use automatically generated content as long as it adds substantial value to the experience and is clearly disclosed.

Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized ai generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized ai generated modelsAs a reminder we have had an AI spam clause in our quality guidelines for over two years: https://t.co/THyyRJarKu

Traditional game systems, including NPC pathfinding, enemy behavior, and procedural level generation, are not classified as generative AI under these rules.

Publisher blames “AI-slop” on Steam as their game only gets 15 players at launch

Almost half of all new Steam games use AI now

Indie dev says Google AI somehow leaked detail about their game that was totally private

The cleanup comes amid growing concerns about AI-generated games on Steam, where an analysis of approximately 63,600 releases found that 49.9% of games launched in October 2026 disclosed using AI, compared to just 1.7% in January 2024.

Some developers have also raised concerns about how the increasing number of submissions could affect smaller studios.

On November 2, indie publisher 2 Left Thumbs blamed a “tidal wave of AI-slop” for allegedly overwhelming Steam’s review process and delaying the release of its co-op game Wheel Make It.

Despite accumulating more than 11,000 wishlists before launch, the game peaked at just 15 concurrent players in the 24 hours after its November 1 release.

The publisher argued that the delay damaged the game’s launch visibility, although Valve has not confirmed that AI-generated submissions were responsible for the review backlog.

#10778. 9 Checks Before Shipping a Product Email: A Workflow for Developers and Designers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A product email can look correct in a design file and still fail its reader. The primary action may disappear when images are blocked. A long workspace name may break the layout. A staging link may survive into production. Even when the message renders correctly, the application may send it twice.

These failures cross design, frontend, backend, and delivery boundaries. A useful release process checks each boundary independently and records what the tests actually establish.

This article uses a workspace invitation as an example. The recipient needs to understand who invited them, identify the workspace, and open a valid acceptance link. The same workflow applies to account notifications, activity summaries, and many other product emails.

Write a short behavioral contract before designing the template:

This separates visual preferences from required behavior. A rounded button is a design choice; a usable invitation link is a requirement.

Build fixtures for a short workspace name, a long name, an accented inviter name, missing optional information, and a translated version. Use synthetic recipients and tokens.

Designers should review these fixtures early. A layout approved only with ideal copy leaves developers to invent overflow behavior later.

MJML provides email-oriented components that compile to responsive HTML. React Email offers a component-based workflow suited to teams already using React.

Choose according to the team’s maintenance needs. Introducing both usually adds complexity without helping a single template.

Regardless of authoring tool, review the generated HTML. The compiled document is what the sending pipeline passes onward, and it can differ substantially from the source component.

Check that the output contains the expected heading, action URL, image alternatives, language information, and footer. Confirm that production rendering uses the same dependency versions as the reviewed build.

SitePoint’s HTML email coding guide provides useful background on email markup. Treat older examples as starting points and verify compatibility against the clients your audience actually uses.

Avoid adding application JavaScript to an email template. Put interactive workflows on a web page and use the email to explain and link to the next action.

Browser support and email-client support are different things. A layout working in Chrome does not establish that it works in every Outlook or Gmail environment.

Use Can I Email to investigate the HTML and CSS features your design depends on. Read the support notes and test dates, not only the headline support percentage.

Define a small client matrix using available audience evidence. Record the specific client and platform; “Outlook” alone is too broad to describe a test environment.

For the invitation example, the baseline should preserve:

SitePoint’s HTML email tips and tricks offers additional implementation context.

Design the baseline first. Decorative effects can improve the experience, but they should not carry information that disappears when a client ignores a CSS rule.

Use visible text for the essential message. A large image containing the entire invitation fails when images are unavailable and gives readers less control over text presentation.

Give meaningful images appropriate alternatives, and use empty alternative text for purely decorative images. Choose descriptive link labels such as “Accept your workspace invitation” instead of repeating “Click here.”

Two useful tools address different questions:

Neither establishes accessibility across every email client. A client may modify markup or colors after delivery.

Manually inspect reading order, text enlargement, keyboard access to links, and the message with images unavailable. Check the delivered email with relevant assistive technology when that is part of your supported environment.

For dark mode, examine the actual resulting colors. Changing a browser preview’s preferred color scheme does not reproduce every email client’s color transformations.

A template preview tests the template. It does not verify that the application selects the right recipient, subject, language, or invitation token.

Route development email to Mailpit, a local SMTP testing tool, and trigger the real application flow using synthetic data.

Mailpit also provides HTML compatibility and link-checking features. Review what a link checker will request before using it on action URLs. An automated request should not consume a single-use invitation or trigger a state-changing action.

A successful capture proves that the development application generated a message. It does not prove that a production mailbox provider will accept it or place it in the inbox.

A perfectly rendered email with a localhost link is still broken.

For a specific invitation flow, an explicit destination validator can catch common mistakes before rendering. The following example assumes invitations must use HTTPS, a single approved hostname, an exact path, and a token:

Run this standalone example with node --test invitation-url.test.mjs. Replace the hostname and route with your application’s documented contract before integrating it.

This checks URL shape, not token authenticity, expiry, or authorization. The receiving application must enforce those properties.

Apply the validator before inserting the URL into a template, and use context-appropriate escaping during rendering. Inspect the final delivered link too, because a sending provider may rewrite it for tracking.

Playwright is useful for repeatable checks against a rendered HTML preview. Test narrow widths, long content, missing optional fields, and the presence of essential text and links.

A browser test can assert that the action has the expected accessible name and destination. It can also capture screenshots for human review.

Keep the limitation explicit: browser automation does not emulate an email client’s HTML rewriting or all of its rendering behavior.

Use an email-client testing service such as Litmus, or controlled test accounts in the clients you support, to inspect the delivered result. Include light and dark appearances where relevant.

Record the template version and fixture alongside each preview. Otherwise, a designer and developer may approve screenshots from different builds.

Do not accept screenshot updates automatically. A changed image may reveal a genuine regression, including truncated text or a button that no longer looks actionable.

Email generation often happens in a background job. That means the release process must account for retries and partial failures.

Give the business event a stable identifier. Record which invitation event produced which send attempt, and use your queue or provider’s documented deduplication mechanisms where available.

Do not promise exactly-once sending merely because a database flag says “sent.” A crash between provider acceptance and saving that flag creates an ambiguous state.

Preserve enough event history to investigate that ambiguity without logging raw invitation tokens. Also separate “accepted by the sending provider” from “delivered to the receiving system,” and from “seen by the user.”

Rendering quality and delivery behavior require separate evidence. Review authentication, bounce handling, complaint signals, suppression behavior, and provider feedback before increasing production volume.

Start with the relevant mailbox provider’s requirements. For example, Gmail’s sender guidelines explain authentication and other requirements, with additional obligations for bulk senders. Check the requirements for your actual sending pattern rather than treating one checklist as universal.

For vendor research at this stage, treat vendor-published comparisons as vendor-authored material: evaluate their claims against provider policies and your own delivery evidence.

Warmup activity is not a substitute for appropriate recipient expectations, correct authentication, or operational monitoring. It also cannot establish that a template is accessible or that an invitation token is valid.

Choose tools according to the question being investigated. A compatibility lookup explains feature support; an SMTP capture shows message construction; a client preview shows rendering; provider events describe delivery outcomes. Keeping those responsibilities clear makes failures easier to diagnose.

A release is ready when the team can explain what the message does, demonstrate the important failure cases, and identify which evidence supports each conclusion.

#10774. NASA’s Perseverance rover completes the first AI-planned drive on Mars

The team behind NASA's six-wheeled Mars explorer tested a vision-enabled artificial intelligence system to map a safe route across the Martian surface without relying on human route planners.

NASA's Perseverance rover has now completed the first drives on another planet that were planned by artificial intelligence. The milestone demonstration took place on Dec. 8 and 10 and was led by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. During the test, generative AI was used to select waypoints for the rover, a complex planning task that is normally handled by human experts on Earth.

"This demonstration shows how far our capabilities have advanced and broadens how we will explore other worlds," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Autonomous technologies like this can help missions to operate more efficiently, respond to challenging terrain, and increase science return as distance from Earth grows. It's a strong example of teams applying new technology carefully and responsibly in real operations."

How Vision AI Helped Navigate the Martian Surface

For the demonstration, engineers used a form of generative AI known as vision-language models to examine existing data from JPL's surface mission dataset. The system analyzed the same images and information that human planners typically use, then identified waypoint locations so Perseverance could travel safely across difficult Martian terrain.

The work was coordinated from JPL's Rover Operations Center (ROC) and carried out in collaboration with Anthropic, using the company's Claude AI models.

Mars sits an average of about 140 million miles (225 million kilometers) from Earth. That distance creates long communication delays, making real-time control of a rover impossible. For nearly three decades, rover navigation has depended on human drivers who carefully study terrain data and plan routes in advance.

These planners design paths made up of waypoints, usually spaced no more than 330 feet (100 meters) apart, to reduce the risk of encountering hazards. The completed plans are sent through NASA's Deep Space Network, and the rover carries out the instructions on its own.

AI Takes Over Route Planning for Perseverance

During Perseverance's drives on the 1,707 and 1,709 Martian days, known as sols, the mission team shifted that responsibility to generative AI. The system examined high-resolution orbital images captured by the HiRISE (High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, along with terrain slope data from digital elevation models.

Using this information, the AI identified important surface features such as bedrock, outcrops, boulder fields, and sand ripples. It then produced a continuous driving path that included all necessary waypoints.

Before sending the commands to Mars, engineers ran the AI-generated instructions through JPL's digital twin (virtual replica of the rover). This step checked more than 500,000 telemetry variables to ensure the plan would work safely with Perseverance's flight software.

On Dec. 8, Perseverance traveled 689 feet (210 meters) using the AI-generated plan. Two days later, it drove another 807 feet (246 meters).

What This Means for Future Space Exploration

"The fundamental elements of generative AI are showing a lot of promise in streamlining the pillars of autonomous navigation for off-planet driving: perception (seeing the rocks and ripples), localization (knowing where we are), and planning and control (deciding and executing the safest path)," said Vandi Verma, a space roboticist at JPL and a member of the Perseverance engineering team. "We are moving towards a day where generative AI and other smart tools will help our surface rovers handle kilometer-scale drives while minimizing operator workload, and flag interesting surface features for our science team by scouring huge volumes of rover images."

"Imagine intelligent systems not only on the ground at Earth, but also in edge applications in our rovers, helicopters, drones, and other surface elements trained with the collective wisdom of our NASA engineers, scientists, and astronauts," said Matt Wallace, manager of JPL's Exploration Systems Office. "That is the game-changing technology we need to establish the infrastructure and systems required for a permanent human presence on the Moon and take the U.S. to Mars and beyond."

Managed for NASA by Caltech, JPL is home to the Rover Operations Center (ROC). The laboratory also oversees daily operations of the Perseverance rover for NASA's Science Mission Directorate as part of the agency's Mars Exploration Program portfolio.

#10772. “Existential risk” – Why scientists are racing to define consciousness

As artificial intelligence continues to advance and ethical concerns grow alongside it, scientists say the need to understand consciousness has reached a critical point.

In a new review published in Frontiers in Science, researchers warn that progress in AI and neurotechnology is moving faster than scientific understanding of consciousness. This gap, they argue, could lead to serious ethical problems if it is not addressed.

The authors say explaining how consciousness emerges is now an urgent scientific and moral priority. A clearer understanding could eventually make it possible to develop scientific methods for detecting consciousness. That breakthrough would have far-reaching consequences for AI development, prenatal policy, animal welfare, medicine, mental health care, law, and emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces.

"Consciousness science is no longer a purely philosophical pursuit. It has real implications for every facet of society -- and for understanding what it means to be human," said lead author Prof Axel Cleeremans from Université Libre de Bruxelles. "Understanding consciousness is one of the most substantial challenges of 21st-century science -- and it's now urgent due to advances in AI and other technologies.

"If we become able to create consciousness -- even accidentally -- it would raise immense ethical challenges and even existential risk," added Cleeremans, a European Research Council (ERC) grantee.

Consciousness, commonly described as awareness of both the world around us and ourselves, remains one of science's most difficult puzzles. Despite decades of research, scientists still lack agreement on how subjective experience emerges from biological processes.

Researchers have identified brain regions and neural activity linked to conscious experience, but major disagreements remain. Scientists continue to debate which brain systems are truly necessary for consciousness and how they interact to produce awareness. Some researchers even question whether this approach captures the problem correctly.

The new review examines the current state of consciousness science, future directions for the field, and the possible consequences if humans succeed in fully explaining or even creating consciousness. This includes the possibility of consciousness emerging in machines or in lab-grown brain-like systems known as "brain organoids."

The authors argue that developing evidence-based tests for consciousness could transform how awareness is identified across many contexts. Such tools could help detect consciousness in patients with brain injuries or dementia and determine when awareness arises in fetuses, animals, brain organoids, or even AI systems.

While this would represent a major scientific advance, the researchers caution that it would also create difficult ethical and legal questions. Determining that a system is conscious would force society to reconsider how that system should be treated.

"Progress in consciousness science will reshape how we see ourselves and our relationship to both artificial intelligence and the natural world," said co-author Prof Anil Seth from the University of Sussex and ERC grantee. "The question of consciousness is ancient -- but it's never been more urgent than now."

A deeper understanding of consciousness could have wide-ranging effects across society.

In medicine, it could improve care for patients who are unresponsive and assumed to be unconscious. Measurements inspired by integrated information theory and global workspace theory[1] have already detected signs of awareness in some individuals diagnosed with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome. Further progress could refine these tools to better assess consciousness in coma, advanced dementia, and anesthesia, and influence treatment decisions and end-of-life care.

Mental health treatment could also benefit. Understanding the biological basis of subjective experience may help researchers develop better therapies for conditions such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia by narrowing the gap between animal studies and human emotional experience.

Greater insight into consciousness could reshape how humans think about their moral responsibilities toward animals. Identifying which animals and systems are sentient could influence animal research practices, farming, food consumption, and conservation strategies. "Understanding the nature of consciousness in particular animals would transform how we treat them and emerging biological systems that are being synthetically generated by scientists," said co-author Prof Liad Mudrik from Tel Aviv University and ERC grantee.

Consciousness research could also affect how the legal system understands responsibility. New findings may challenge traditional legal concepts such as mens rea, the "guilty mind" required to establish intent. As neuroscience reveals how much behavior arises from unconscious processes, courts may need to reconsider where responsibility begins and ends.

At the same time, advances in AI, brain organoids, and brain-computer interfaces raise the possibility of creating or altering awareness beyond natural biological limits. While some researchers believe consciousness might arise through computation alone, others argue that biological factors play an essential role. "Even if 'conscious AI' is impossible using standard digital computers, AI that gives the impression of being conscious raises many societal and ethical challenges," said Seth.

The authors emphasize the need for a coordinated, evidence-based approach to studying consciousness. One proposed strategy involves adversarial collaborations, in which competing theories are tested against each other through experiments designed jointly by their supporters. "We need more team science to break theoretical silos and overcome existing biases and assumptions," said Mudrik. "This step has the potential to move the field forward."

The researchers also argue that scientific work should place greater emphasis on phenomenology (what consciousness feels like) alongside studies of function (what consciousness does).

"Cooperative efforts are essential to make progress -- and to ensure society is prepared for the ethical, medical, and technological consequences of understanding, and perhaps creating, consciousness," said Cleeremans.

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
